passages.section: S.6 Building Digital Twin of Commercial dToF LiDAR
passages.location: S.6 Building Digital Twin of Commercial dToF LiDAR
passages.text: To demonstrate VisionSIM’s ability to bridge the real-to-sim gap we conducted an experiment in which we implemented a perceptual digital twin and verified its accuracy with respect it’s real world counterpart (as described in Sec. 5 ).

For this evaluation we captured the real scene using an off-the-shelf, commercial, single photon LiDAR developed by ADAPs Photonics [ 1 ] (the ADS6311) used because it gives access to raw unprocessed histograms. The ADS6311 is a 1D scanning LiDAR with a resolution of 256 × 192 256\times 192 with 3 × 3 3\times 3 spatial binning to improve SNR (i.e. there are 768 × 576 768\times 576 SPAD elements). This device has a dead-time of ∼ 11 {\raise 0.73193pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}11 ns and a temporal resolution of 754 754 ps. The transmitter uses VCSEL laser diodes to scan a 6-row-wide band in the vertical direction.

We set up a scene in lab with a retroreflective stop sign. Retroreflector’s send incident light back towards its source resulting in two phenomena: pileup and glare (referred to as bloom in the LiDAR community). Pileup is the result of a SPAD element’s ”dead-time” which biases the sensor toward earlier detections. In the event of strong returns such as those from a retroreflector, this bias is strengthened which leads to what is referred as range walk error (an error in the measured depth) as well as a reduction in measured intensity (due to photons in later time bins being missed). In addition to causing pileup, some of the returning waveform scatters diffusely on the lens as well as bouncing between the lens, receiver housing, and pixel array which all lead to spurious detections. This is the cause of what is known as glare or bloom (in traditional CMOS imaging this is sometimes called lens flare).
This evaluation gave us the ability to determine if VisionSIM could faithfully reconstruct the artifacts stemming from the physical acquisition process which is demonstrated in Figure 4 .

We then reconstructed this scene in Blender with the stop sign and background at roughly the same depth and dimensions. Also, with the camera at the same position as it was when we captured the real scene. This is not a perfect reconstruction as the ADAPs kit provides only opencv-style coefficients which Blender does not follow for their barrel distorted lenses. Thus, we used a lens and camera model that was a perceptually similar approximation to the ADS6311. Additionally, currently VisionSIM does not directly support retroreflective objects; to overcome this we used the material identifiers and manually set albedo to approximate the extremely high albedo of retroreflectors (as well as the comparatively low albedo of the background, a black canvas tarp).

passages.text: To simulate the glare artifacts we measured the PSF function of the ADS6311 by disabling the transmitter and pointing an IR flashlight at the same wavelength toward the receiver. We used a small aperture and baffle to ensure light was incident on a single pixel and that there were no multipath effects being measured respectively. These 49 measured PSF’s are treated as a basis, with remaining positions interpolated by a distance-weighted sum of the 49 measured positions. We plan to add more robust lens modeling that includes a parametric form of this glare model and can be learned in a similar fashion to the IRF learning described in section S.6.3 . Error maps for each additional modeled effect (IRF, pileup, and bloom) can be found in Figure 4 . It should be noted that the discrepancy between the reported RMSE from the main paper and this figure is due to a tighter crop around the region of interest. This is in part to highlight the effects of our realistic modeling but also because the background tarp was the most challenging to match in Blender, causing error unrelated to VisionSIMs physical model but instead due to imperfections in how the ground truth depth was calculated for the tarp in Blender.

Asset curation. To help accelerate research, we release all 3 3 D assets and scripts used to create sensor-realistic datasets, lowering the need for manual asset curation, which can be a significant hurdle. Specifically, we release the 100 100 high-quality rigged scenes, some of which are shown in Fig. 5 , which have been used to create the VisionSIM dataset. These scenes have mostly been crowdsourced from sites such as BlendSwap [ 60 ] or Blender’s example scenes [ 4 ] , although some have been made or heavily modified specifically for this use case. All scenes are fully rigged, physics-baked, and validated to render without modification using the Blender version pinned to the corresponding VisionSIM release. These assets are released under the Creative Commons license (CC BY 4.0) or similar permissive licenses.

Generation pipeline. Dataset generation is driven by a single script, scripts/mkdataset.py , that wraps the same RenderConfig dataclass and render_animation backend used throughout VisionSIM’s CLI. A user specifies a directory of blend-files and an output directory; the script then (i) uniformly samples non-overlapping sub-trajectories from the animation range of each scene, or renders the whole trajectory if desired, (ii) dispatches each (scene, trajectory) pair as an asynchronous render job via BlenderClients.pool , and (iii) saves every sequence under a deterministic path which also contains the explicit configuration used to produce the sequence. All relevant metadata are stored in per-modality SQLite databases alongside the raw data. The RenderConfig dataclass exposes every relevant parameter — resolution, render device, keyframe multiplier, types of ground truth, noise threshold, and per-modality flags — entirely through the CLI, so a full reconfiguration of the dataset requires no code changes. For the full dataset, this script was submitted to HTCondor [ 12 ] via a containerized VisionSIM image, distributing work across thousands of CPUs and hundreds of GPUs as described in Appendix S.2 . Sensor emulation (interpolation, SPC, event camera, iToF, thermal, IMU) is applied as a post-processing pass on the ground-truth renders using the same VisionSIM library functions described in Appendix S.3 , each of which has a corresponding command-line interface tool.

Reproducibility. Every VisionSIM release is containerized with Docker [ 57 ] and tested end-to-end in CI, ensuring that a pinned version of the library and its container can regenerate all data without any environment configuration. Users who wish to reproduce or modify the dataset only need to (i) pull the versioned Docker image corresponding to the release tag, (ii) obtain the released blend-files, and (iii) invoke mkdataset.py with the published configuration.
